subject: zoology
question_text: What are the deleterious effects of depletion of ozone in the stratosphere?

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.46, SAQ 55). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

steps.label: Depletion of the ozone layer
lines: The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere and
absorbs the ultraviolet (UV) radiation of
sunlight.
When the ozone layer is depleted markedly it
leads to an ozone hole.
The layer becomes very thin and can no
longer stop the UV radiation completely.
The shorter wavelength rays, UV-B, then
reach the earth's surface.
steps.why: Every harmful effect that follows is caused by UV-B, so this step must get the radiation to the ground first; an answer that lists the effects without naming UV-B has left out the cause.
common_mistakes: Writing that the ozone hole itself burns the skin. The harm is done by the UV-B that passes through.
Naming UV-A. The harmful shorter wavelength radiation here is UV-B.
steps.memory_tip: Thin layer, more UV-B through, and every effect below follows from that one fact.
steps.margin_note: Get UV-B to the ground before listing any effect. Four short lines.

steps.label: Effect on DNA
lines: UV rays damage the DNA of the cells.
This may lead to mutations.
Mutations change the working of the cell and
can be passed on when the cell divides.
steps.why: DNA damage is placed first among the effects because it is the deepest one — the changes to the skin and the eyes are what a person sees, but the damage begins in the molecule.
common_mistakes: Writing that UV kills the cell outright. It DAMAGES the DNA and causes mutations.
Leaving out the word mutation, which is the named result here.
steps.memory_tip: Work from the inside out: DNA first, then the skin, then the eyes.
steps.margin_note: Two short lines. The word mutation must appear.

steps.label: Effect on the skin
lines: UV rays cause ageing of the skin.
They damage the skin cells and can cause
skin cancer.
They also cause sunburn on exposed skin.
steps.why: Skin cancer is the effect examiners look for by name, so it is written in full rather than being left inside a general statement about damage.
common_mistakes: Writing damage to the skin without naming skin cancer.
Writing that UV causes leprosy or any infection. UV damage is not an infection.
steps.memory_tip: Skin gets three things from UV: it ages, it burns, and it may turn cancerous.
steps.margin_note: Three short effects. Skin cancer must be named in words.

steps.label: Effect on the eyes

lines.text: UV-B harms the DNA, the skin and the eyes

lines: A high concentration of UV-B causes
inflammation of the cornea.
This leads to snow blindness and to
cataract.
Sometimes it damages the cornea permanently.
steps.why: The eye effects are the ones with named conditions attached, and naming the cornea shows exactly which part of the eye is struck, which is what separates a full answer from a vague one.
common_mistakes: Writing that UV causes blindness. The named conditions are snow blindness and cataract.
Naming the retina. The part named in this answer is the CORNEA.
steps.memory_tip: Three eye words in order: cornea inflamed, snow blindness, cataract.
steps.margin_note: Name the cornea and both conditions. The box gathers the three targets of UV-B.

insider_note: Every effect must be traced back to UV-B — an answer that says the ozone hole causes cancer without naming the radiation loses the first mark.
